stances.claim: Although the Philippines commanded less than 3 percent of Aria's text, the law is structurally useful to advance PH national interest because its core themes -- rules-based order, universal human rights, transparent governance, free markets, peaceful dispute resolution backed by strong military presence -- align with the Philippine Constitution.
stances.rhetorical_move: policy-alignment argument (using textual overlap between foreign law and domestic Constitution as cooperative leverage)

stances.claim: The enduring source of national interest is the Constitution -- its Declaration of Principles, Bill of Rights, and provisions on transparent governance, accountability, equitable wealth distribution, social justice, and education -- not the temporary preferences of any leader, because 'leaders and bosses, patriots and tyrants may come and go but our values endure.'
stances.rhetorical_move: constitution-as-bedrock framing (positioning constitutional values as more durable than political leadership)

stances.claim: PH should align with the US in safeguarding the policies Aria proudly proclaims -- unless specific US actions violate the PH Constitution or other national interests -- using Aria's 'strategic partnership' offer to enforce the 2016 Arbitral Award through Asean.
stances.rhetorical_move: selective-alignment principle (conditional cooperation with explicit constitutional veto)

stances.claim: While the US enforces freedom of navigation citing PH's arbitral victory, America must be reminded not to build its own bases in Scarborough or elsewhere in PH territory, and must join PH in developing WPS resources under the 60/40 constitutional sharing rule.

PH must also engage China -- the new superpower that could overtake the US as the world's top economy -- without being beguiled by loan small prints or antagonizing it, hoping that China's own historical experience of Western colonization will restrain it from becoming the kind of greedy bully it once hated.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical-empathy invocation (asking China to be ruled by memory of its own suffering)

notable_anecdotes: CJ's invocation of 'Pambansang Awit' and 'Bayan Ko' as 'eternally etched in our psyche' -- rare patriotic-musical reference making the Constitution emotionally rather than merely doctrinally the source of national interest.
The acknowledgment that PH controlled 'less than 3 percent of Aria's text' -- a quietly devastating measure of how marginal PH was in the drafting of the very law it must now leverage.
CJ's framing of China as having 'magnificently risen from its sad history of exploitation by the greedy Western powers' -- the most charitable contextualizing of China's rise in CJ's WPS columns.

The closing prayer that China's 'bitter experience restrain it from becoming one of the greedy bullies it once hated' -- the most rhetorically charged single line, an explicit moral appeal embedded in geopolitical analysis.
Citation of Ambassador Hermenegildo C. Cruz's 'might makes right' formulation (Opinion, March 4, 2020) as the realist baseline against which PH must operate.

one_paragraph_summary: Building on his August 2 column, Panganiban shifts from asking whether the US Asia Reassurance Initiative Act of 2018 (Aria) is enforceable as PH law to asking how PH can use Aria -- which dedicated less than 3 percent of its text to the Philippines -- to advance its own national interest. He invokes the diplomatic maxim that nations 'have no permanent friends or permanent enemies, only permanent interests,' and locates the enduring source of PH national interest in the Constitution: the Declaration of Principles, the Bill of Rights, and the provisions on transparent governance, accountability, social justice, and education that survive every leader and tyrant. Because Aria's stated aspirations -- rules-based order, universal human rights, peaceful dispute resolution backed by 'strong military presence' -- align with the Philippine Constitution, PH should generally cooperate with the US in safeguarding them, while reserving the right to dissent whenever specific US actions violate PH constitutional norms. He urges PH to accept Aria's 'strategic partnership' offer to enforce the 2016 Arbitral Award through Asean, but to insist that America not build bases in Scarborough Shoal or anywhere else on PH territory, and that resource development in the WPS respect the 60/40 constitutional sharing rule. He closes with a parallel posture toward China -- the rising superpower that could soon overtake the US -- calling for engagement without subservience or antagonism, and praying that China's own bitter colonial memory will restrain it 'from becoming one of the greedy bullies it once hated.'
